## About these questions {.unnumbered}

These questions are for extra practice after Lab 5, using the same data.
Each section follows on from the matching task in `lab_05.qmd`, so do that task first.
Questions marked **Extension** are more challenging.

The cell below loads the data we used in the lab.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
simpsons_characters <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_characters.csv")
simpsons_episodes <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_episodes.csv")
simpsons_locations <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_locations.csv")
simpsons_script_lines <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_script_lines.csv")
stock_data <- read_csv("data/all_stocks_5yr.csv") |>
    clean_names()
```

### Joining Data

These questions follow on from Tasks 1 and 1b of the lab.
(Make sure your outputs print character names, not just IDs).

- [ ] Which characters have lines in the most episodes?
- [ ] **Extension:** Which characters appear together most frequently in episodes?

::: {.solution}
*Which characters have lines in the most episodes?*

We count the episodes for each `character_id` first, and only then join to `simpsons_characters` to get the names.
This way the join is done on a small summary table (one row per character) rather than on all 158,255 script lines.

```{r}
simpsons_script_lines |>
    group_by(character_id) |>
    summarise(num_episodes = n_distinct(episode_id), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(num_episodes)) |>
    inner_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id" = "id")) |>
    select(character_name, num_episodes) |>
    head(10)
```

Notice that grouping by `character_id` also creates a group for `NA`, the scene directions with no character (see Task 1 of the lab).
This group appears in 564 episodes, tying with Homer for first place!
The `inner_join` quietly removes it, because `NA` has no match in `simpsons_characters`; with a `left_join` it would appear near the top of the table with no name.
It would be clearer still to remove it on purpose, with `filter(!is.na(character_id))` before grouping.

*Which characters appear together most frequently in episodes?*

First we make a table with one row for each character in each episode, dropping the scene directions (which have no character):

```{r}
episode_characters <- simpsons_script_lines |>
    filter(!is.na(character_id)) |>
    select(episode_id, character_id) |>
    distinct()
```

To find pairs of characters in the same episode, we join this table to *itself* on `episode_id`.
Each episode has many characters on both sides of the join, so this is a many-to-many join: every character in an episode is matched with every other character in that episode.
As the notes say, `dplyr` warns about many-to-many joins because they are often a mistake, but here it is exactly what we want, so we say so with `relationship = "many-to-many"`, which also silences the warning.

```{r}
episode_characters |>
    inner_join(episode_characters, by = "episode_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    # both tables have a character_id column, so they get .x and .y suffixes.
    # Keeping only character_id.x < character_id.y removes each character paired
    # with themselves, and counts each pair once rather than twice (as A-B and B-A).
    filter(character_id.x < character_id.y) |>
    group_by(character_id.x, character_id.y) |>
    summarise(episodes_together = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    # join back to characters twice, to get both names (again with .x and .y suffixes)
    left_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id.x" = "id")) |>
    left_join(simpsons_characters, by = c("character_id.y" = "id")) |>
    select(character_name.x, character_name.y, episodes_together) |>
    arrange(desc(episodes_together)) |>
    head(20)
```
:::

### String Processing

These questions follow on from Task 2 of the lab.

- [ ] How many lines contain exclamation marks?
- [ ] **Extension:** Read about *regular expressions* (see the Regular Expressions tip in the Week 5 notes, and try [regex101](https://regex101.com/)). In the lab you counted the episodes that mention donuts / doughnuts. Answer that question again, this time using a single `str_detect` with a regular expression that matches both "donut" and "doughnut".
- [ ] Some location names are written in capitals (e.g. `KITCHEN`) and others are not (e.g. `Simpson Home`). How many are in capitals? Use `str_to_title` to give all the location names consistent capitalisation. Look through the results: does `str_to_title` always give what you want?

::: {.solution}
*How many lines contain exclamation marks?*
```{r}
simpsons_script_lines |>
    filter(str_detect(spoken_words, "!")) |>
    nrow()
```

*Extension: using a regular expression*

In a regular expression, `|` means "or", so `"donut|doughnut"` matches either word.
As in the lab, we convert the text to lower case first, so that "Donut" and "DONUTS" are matched too.

```{r}
simpsons_script_lines |>
    filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(spoken_words), "donut|doughnut")) |>
    distinct(episode_id) |>
    nrow()
```

A more compact pattern is `"do(ugh)?nut"`: the brackets group `ugh` together, and `?` means "the previous thing is optional", so this matches "donut" and "doughnut".

```{r}
simpsons_script_lines |>
    filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(spoken_words), "do(ugh)?nut")) |>
    distinct(episode_id) |>
    nrow()
```

*Tidying the capitalisation of location names*

A name is written in capitals exactly when converting it to upper case leaves it unchanged:

```{r}
simpsons_locations |>
    filter(location_name == str_to_upper(location_name)) |>
    nrow()
```

That's more than half of the 4,459 locations.
We can use `str_to_title` to put every name in "title case", and look at a few examples:

```{r}
simpsons_locations |>
    mutate(title_name = str_to_title(location_name)) |>
    filter(location_name %in% c("KITCHEN", "Simpson Home", "TV Studio", "Circus of Values", "NEIGHBOR #1'S HOUSE")) |>
    select(location_name, title_name)
```

`str_to_title` simply capitalises the first letter of each word and puts the rest in lower case.
That works well for `KITCHEN`, but it doesn't know that "TV" is an abbreviation or that short words like "of" are usually left in lower case, and it is confused by the apostrophe in `#1'S`.
Names that were already sensibly capitalised can be made *worse*.
One improvement is to convert only the names that are in capitals, using `if_else` (see the Week 2 notes):

```{r}
simpsons_locations |>
    mutate(location_name = if_else(
        location_name == str_to_upper(location_name),
        str_to_title(location_name),
        location_name
    )) |>
    filter(id %in% c(6, 14)) |>
    select(id, location_name)
```

Even so, for names that were entirely in capitals, information such as which words were abbreviations has been lost, and no function can recover it perfectly.
Automatic cleaning like this is usually good enough for display, but it's worth checking the results rather than assuming they are right.
:::

### Dates

These questions follow on from Tasks 3a and 3b of the lab.

In `simpsons_episodes`, `read_csv` has already recognised `original_air_date` as a date.

- [ ] On which day of the week did episodes first air? Is there anything surprising? (Hint: look at the formatting section of the Week 5 notes; the format code for the day of the week is `%A`.)
- [ ] How many years ago did the first episode in the data air?

::: {.solution}
*Which day of the week did episodes first air?*

```{r}
simpsons_episodes |>
    mutate(weekday = format(original_air_date, "%A")) |>
    count(weekday, sort = TRUE)
```

Most episodes aired on a Sunday, but 89 aired on a Thursday.
Counting the Thursday episodes by season shows that they are all from seasons 2 to 5:

```{r}
simpsons_episodes |>
    mutate(weekday = format(original_air_date, "%A")) |>
    filter(weekday == "Thursday") |>
    count(season)
```

In fact, The Simpsons moved to Thursday nights between 1990 and 1994, before moving back to Sundays.

*How many years ago did the first episode air?*

```{r}
first_air_date <- min(simpsons_episodes$original_air_date)
first_air_date
interval(first_air_date, today()) |>
    time_length("years")
```

This answer depends on the day you run the code, since `today()` changes!
:::

The next question uses the stock market data from Task 3b of the lab.

- [ ] What is the average trading volume for each month, across all years?

::: {.solution}
We group by both the month number and the month name.
The name makes the output readable, but on its own it would sort the months alphabetically (April, August, December, ...); including the number keeps them in calendar order.

```{r}
stock_data |>
    mutate(month = month(date), month_name = format(date, "%B")) |>
    group_by(month, month_name) |>
    summarise(mean_volume = mean(volume), .groups = "drop")
```
:::
